The experience of Médecins Sans Frontières in providing antiretroviral therapy in resource-limited settings was documented in the journal AIDS on July 11, 2008, in volume 22, issue 11, pages 1305–1312. 2. Sawé FK and McIntyre JA emphasized the importance of monitoring HIV antiretroviral therapy in resource-limited settings to prevent costly outcomes, as published in Clinical Infectious Diseases on August 1, 2009, volume 49, issue 3, pages 463–465. 3. Gilks CF, Crowley S, Ekpini R, and colleagues discussed the World Health Organization's public health approach to antiretroviral treatment for HIV in resource-limited settings in The Lancet on August 5, 2006, volume 368, issue 9534, pages 505–510. 4. The World Health Organization released consolidated guidelines in 2013 on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection, recommending a public health approach. 5. A second edition of the WHO consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use for HIV treatment and prevention, emphasizing a public health approach, was published in Geneva, Switzerland, in 2016. 6. Kanters S, Socias ME, Paton NI, and colleagues conducted a systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing the efficacy and safety of second-line antiretroviral therapy for HIV/AIDS treatment, published in The Lancet HIV in October 2017, volume 4, issue 10, pages e433–e441. 7. Amin J, Boyd MA, Kumarasamy N, and colleagues demonstrated that raltegravir was non-inferior to nucleoside-based regimens in second-line therapy with lopinavir/ritonavir over 96 weeks in a randomized open-label study for HIV-1 treatment, published in PLOS One in 2015, volume 10, issue 2, article e0118228. 8. The Second-Line Study Group, led by Boyd MA and Kumarasamy N, compared ritonavir-boosted lopinavir with nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors versus ritonavir-boosted lopinavir with raltegravir for HIV-1 treatment in adults experiencing virological failure of standard first-line ART regimens. This randomized, open-label, non-inferiority study was published in The Lancet on June 15, 2013, volume 381, issue 9883, pages 2091–2099. 9. Ciaffi L, Koulla-Shiro S, Sawadogo A, and colleagues evaluated the efficacy and safety of three second-line antiretroviral regimens in HIV-infected patients in Africa, as published in AIDS on July 31, 2015, volume 29, issue 12, pages 1473–1481. 10. The EARNEST Trial Team presented 144-week follow-up results on second-line treatment in sub-Saharan Africa at the 2015 Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI). 11. Hakim J highlighted the impact of NRTI cross-resistance on outcomes of second-line protease inhibitor (PI) plus NRTI therapy in Africa, presented at CROI 2015. 12. Paton NI, Kityo C, Hoppe A, and colleagues assessed second-line antiretroviral regimens for HIV therapy in Africa, with findings published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2014, volume 371, issue 3, pages 234–247. 13. Higgins JP, Altman DG, Gotzsche PC, and colleagues developed the Cochrane Collaboration's tool for assessing the risk of bias in randomized trials, published in BMJ in 2011, volume 343, article d5928. 14. Dias S, Welton N, Sutton A, and Ades A provided a technical support document outlining a generalized linear modeling framework for pairwise and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in 2011. 15. Guyatt GH, Oxman AD, Kunz R, and colleagues published GRADE guidelines for rating the quality of evidence, focusing on imprecision, inconsistency, publication bias, and indirectness, in Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in December 2011, volume 64, issues 12, pages 1277–1316. 16. Puhan MA, Schunemann HJ, Murad MH, and colleagues described the GRADE Working Group's approach for rating the quality of treatment effect estimates from network meta-analyses in BMJ in 2014, volume 349, article g5630. 17. Aboud M, Brites C, Lu H, and colleagues presented outcomes of dolutegravir versus lopinavir/ritonavir in second-line therapy (DAWNING study) at the 2018 CROI in Boston, USA. 18. Amin J reported that raltegravir was non-inferior to the standard of care in second-line therapy over 96 weeks, as discussed in Topics in Antiviral Medicine in April 2014, volume 22, issue E-1, pages 259–260. 19. Boyd MA, Kumarasamy N, Moore CL, and colleagues compared ritonavir-boosted lopinavir with nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors versus ritonavir-boosted lopinavir with raltegravir for HIV-1 treatment in adults with virological failure of first-line ART regimens, published in The Lancet on June 15, 2013, volume 381, issue 9883, pages 2091–2099. 20. Bunupuradah T, Chetchotisakd P, Ananworanich J, and colleagues conducted a randomized comparison of second-line lopinavir/ritonavir monotherapy versus tenofovir/lamivudine/lopinavir/ritonavir in patients failing NNRTI regimens, published in Antiviral Therapy in 2012, volume 17, issue 7, pages 1351–1361. 21. Hakim JG, Thompson J, Kityo C, and colleagues reported 144-week follow-up results from the EARNEST trial on second-line treatment of HIV, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in January 2018, volume 18, issue 1, pages 47–57. 22. Koulla-Shiro S, Ciaffi L, Le Moing V, and colleagues compared three second-line ART regimens in Africa in the 2LADY Study, presented at the 2014 CROI in Boston, USA. 23. La Rosa AM, Harrison LJ, Taiwo B, and colleagues evaluated raltegravir in second-line antiretroviral therapy in resource-limited settings in the SELECT study, published in The Lancet HIV in June 2016, volume 3, issue 6, pages e247–258. 24. Patel AK, Patel KK, Naik E, and colleagues compared the effectiveness of low-dose indinavir/ritonavir versus atazanavir/ritonavir-based generic ART in NNRTI-experienced HIV-1-infected patients in India, published in Journal of the International Association of Physicians in AIDS Care in March-April 2011, volume 10, issue 2, pages 111–118. 25. The World Health Organization provided guidance on transitioning to dolutegravir use, accessed online in June 2018. 26. Wiznia A, Alvero C, Fenton T, and colleagues presented 48-week results of dolutegravir in HIV-infected children aged 6–12 years (IMPACT 1093) at the 2016 CROI in Boston, USA. 27. Viani RM, Alvero C, Fenton T, and colleagues reported on the safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy of dolutegravir in treatment-experienced HIV-1-infected adolescents, published in The Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal in 2015, volume 34, issue 11, pages 1207–1213. 28. UNAIDS announced the launch of high-quality antiretroviral therapy in South Africa, Kenya, and over 90 lowand middle-income countries at reduced prices in 2017.
